title: SciAgentGym: Benchmarking Multi-Step Scientific Tool-Use in LLM Agents
claim: A single worked trajectory shows an agent orchestrating tools, recovering from errors, and synthesizing a final answer in an interactive environment.
layout: 3 stacked regions: task on top, agent and environment panels side by side, output below
description: The figure is a worked example of one agent trajectory on a chemistry task. A top box with a question-mark icon states the task (pick the best rod-shaped ligand), the sub-question (minimize a score built from asphericity and eccentricity), and four candidate molecules. Below it, the left panel, headed "Agent.step" with a cartoon scientist, lists actions and tool calls in colored cards. Green cards mark successful steps and carry teal checkmarks. A red card with a warning triangle shows a missing-parameter error. The next green card is the error recovery. Small scatter and bar charts show the candidate comparison. The right panel, "Environment", lists the dataset, toolkit, files and code, plus an execution log with step and tool-call counts. A green arrow labeled "read" leads to the bottom Output box. That box gives the answer, the score arithmetic, and molecule structure images. The eye goes first to the top task box, then down the green and red cards.
caption: Benchmarking multi-step scientific tool-use in SciAgentGym. A representative trajectory where an LLM agent interacts with the environment to solve a complex chemistry task. This example illustrates the core agent capabilities demonstrated within our environment: orchestrating domain-specific tools, recovering from errors, and synthesizing final outputs.
abstract: Scientific reasoning inherently demands integrating sophisticated toolkits to navigate domain-specific knowledge. Yet, current benchmarks largely overlook agents' ability to orchestrate tools for such rigorous workflows. To bridge this gap, we introduce SciAgentGym, a scalable interactive environment featuring 1,780 domain-specific tools across four natural science disciplines, supported by a robust execution infrastructure. Complementing this, we present SciAgentBench, a tiered evaluation suite designed to stress-test agentic capabilities from elementary actions to long-horizon workflows. Our evaluation identifies a critical bottleneck: state-of-the-art models still struggle with complex scientific tool-use, and their performance degrades substantially as interaction horizons extend. To address this, we propose SciForge, a data synthesis method that models the tool action space as a dependency graph to generate logic-aware training trajectories. By fine-tuning on these trajectories, our SciAgent-8B outperforms the significantly larger Qwen3-VL-235B-Instruct while exhibiting positive cross-domain transfer of scientific tool-use capabilities. These results underscore the promising potential of next-generation autonomous scientific agents.
